paper_did: Utilized hybrid Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics (MC/MD) simulations on an equimolar TaNbHfZr refractory high‐entropy alloy (HEA) to mimic high‐temperature annealing (at 1800 °C) and study nanostructure evolution (including the formation of chemical short‐range clusters, SRCs) via sequential MC swaps.

Employed atomistic simulations (with cells of 48,000 atoms and larger replicated cells) to analyze the evolution of thermodynamic properties—tracking changes in enthalpy (ΔH) and Gibbs free energy (ΔG) as a function of MC swap count—and linked these changes to the formation of SRCs.

Inserted edge dislocations (½[1 1 1] type) into both the initial random and evolved alloy structures to simulate dislocation glide behavior under applied shear and estimate the critically resolved shear stress (CRSS), thereby relating nanostructural changes to yield strength enhancement and elucidating atomistic dislocation reactions and pinning mechanisms.
paper_reported: That the MC/MD simulated annealing induces significant SRC formation which reduces the system’s ΔH by about 75–80 meV/atom and ΔG by roughly 45 meV/atom, with the free‐energy change converging after ~20 MC swaps – a trend that correlates with experimental observations of annealed alloys.

A rapid increase in CRSS from ~435 MPa in the random solid solution to ~815 MPa after 10 MC swaps, leading to predicted yield strengths (via Taylor factor conversion) in close agreement (<8% deviation) with experimental measurements for both as-synthesized and annealed samples.

Detailed atomistic mechanisms of dislocation–SRC interaction, including dislocation core dissociation, loop formation, and reactions (e.g., the emergence of [1 0 0] segments), which underpin the observed strengthening and the onset of ductile-to-brittle transition behavior.
paper_proposed: Future investigations aimed at further elucidating the stability of dislocations and lattice structures under high shear to explain the ductile-to-brittle transition, suggesting the potential for extending the computational framework to more comprehensive thermodynamic and mechanistic studies.

paper_did: Measured the temperature‐dependent molar heat capacity (cp) of single‐phase high entropy alloys (HEAs) – including single‐crystalline nickel and the equiatomic Cantor alloy, as well as several other fcc, bcc, and hcp alloys – over a wide temperature range (from –170 °C up to near the solidus temperature).

Performed differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) experiments using different setups (alumina crucibles and Pt-Rh crucibles with ceramic liners) under inert atmospheres, with careful pre-treatments such as etching and fine grinding to ensure good thermal contact.

Applied extrapolation methods (e.g., fitting cp ∝ T³ at low temperatures) and compared experimental cp values with predictions by the rule of mixture (and the Dulong–Petit law), subsequently calculating the thermal entropy (Sₜₕₑᵣₘₐₗ) and total entropy (S_total = S_conf + Sₜₕₑᵣₘₐₗ).

Analyzed the contributions to the Gibbs free energy by separating the thermal and configurational parts, and demonstrated that although Sₜₕₑᵣₘₐₗ is large and similar for alloys with the same crystal structure, only the configurational entropy (S_conf) induces the reduction in ΔG that stabilizes a multicomponent solid‐solution phase.
paper_reported: Room-temperature cp values for the alloys are close to 3R, in accordance with the Dulong–Petit law, and the rule-of-mixture predictions match well with the experimental data.
Distinct features in the cp curves (such as the Curie peak in pure nickel and a plateau-like feature in the Cantor alloy) that are attributed to magnetic transitions were observed.

DSC data indicate that while thermal entropy is the major contribution to the absolute value of entropy, differences in configurational entropy govern the compositional dependence of the Gibbs free energy, thereby stabilizing the solid-solution phase in HEAs.
Challenges at high temperatures were noted for some alloys due to chemical reactions with the crucible and environment, leading to uncertainties in determining the melting intervals for certain HEAs.
paper_proposed: Future studies should verify the hypothesis that magnetic ordering – especially in alloys like the hcp system with 4f electron contributions – affects the measured heat capacity.

An in-depth investigation of the ‘mixing paradox’ is suggested to study the impact of atomic size differences in solid solutions, with particular attention to dislocation movement and related mechanical properties.

paper_did: Synthesized Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy via arc melting using high‐purity elemental powders with multiple re-melting cycles and mechanical cleaning to ensure homogeneity.

Subjected the alloy to three distinct cooling conditions: slow cooling on a copper plate (~52 K/s), accelerated cooling via a short electric arc pulse (~3018 K/s), and rapid quenching using the melt-spinning method (10⁵–10⁶ K/s).
Characterized the resulting microstructures using XRD, SEM, TEM, and Mössbauer spectroscopy.
Performed thermal analyses using differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) and thermographic measurements to trace phase transformation temperatures and cooling profiles.
paper_reported: DSC analysis revealed two endothermic peaks during heating (one associated with a pre-melting event and one with full melting) and corresponding exothermic events during cooling that indicate crystallization processes.

XRD, SEM, and TEM confirmed that slow and accelerated cooling produced multiphase crystalline microstructures (e.g., FCC, tetragonal, orthorhombic phases), whereas melt-spinning resulted in an amorphous structure with short-range order.

Mössbauer spectroscopy provided insights into the local atomic environment of iron, showing a paramagnetic state in all conditions with variations in electric field asymmetry correlating with cooling rate and microstructural order.

paper_did: Conducted high-throughput CALPHAD calculations on over 130,000 multi‐component alloy systems (filtered to ≈5,540 credible, equimolar systems with fAB = 1) to generate phase diagrams for HEAs with 3–6 elements.

Developed a computational screening framework to identify promising alloy systems for high‐temperature structural applications.
paper_reported: Found that the fraction of solid solution alloys decreases and the probability of IM or mixed phases increases with increasing number of alloying elements, contradicting the traditional entropy stabilization argument for HEAs.
Showed quantitative trends such as decreasing extreme property ranges (e.g., Tm, Tuse, density, modulus) with increasing alloy complexity, and detailed how phase counts vary with composition.
Identified 51 candidate equimolar alloy systems (with 3–6 elements) that meet a set of stringent design criteria for high-temperature structural applications.
paper_proposed: Extend the alloy exploration beyond the equimolar composition space to non-equimolar alloys in order to discover compositions with potentially more extreme properties.

fields.hypothesis: Apply an isothermal–isobaric interface pinning method to directly compute free energy differences between the solid and liquid phases of HEAs, thereby accurately determining melting temperatures, latent heats, fusion entropies, and volume changes without relying solely on two-phase coexistence.

fields.intervention: Introduce a bias (pinning) field into the simulation to hold a stable solid–liquid interface. Use thermodynamic integration to compute the free energy difference between the phases as a function of temperature. Determine Tm at the point where ΔG = 0, and extract ΔHfusion and ΔSfusion from the integrated free energy curves.
fields.conditions: Simulations run at constant pressure in cells large enough (~50,000 atoms) to accommodate a well-defined pinned interface; the pinning field must be optimized to minimally perturb the intrinsic energies while maintaining interface stability.
fields.structural_mediator: The solid–liquid interface where the distinct free energy landscapes of SRC-equipped solid and the disordered liquid are directly compared.
fields.mechanism: By anchoring the interface via a pinning field, the approach minimizes hysteresis and interface drift, enabling precise computation of the free energy difference between phases. This method naturally incorporates the effects of SRC-induced configurational ordering on the free energy of the solid while capturing the disordered nature of the liquid, leading to accurate prediction of fusion thermodynamic properties.
fields.predicted_outcome: Melting temperatures, latent heats, and fusion entropies computed via interface pinning are expected to deviate by less than 7–10% from experimental values. The method will efficiently resolve how SRC alters the free energy balance across the interface.
fields.baseline: Earlier MC/MD approaches equilibrated solid structures via MC swaps without a controlled means of pinning the interface, making free energy differences less directly accessible.
fields.boundary: Success relies on the proper tuning of the pinning field and may be limited if the interface becomes excessively unstable in highly disordered liquid regions.
fields.uncertainty: The sensitivity of computed free energies to the details of the bias field and the inherent variability of SRC in the solid introduces uncertainties that require careful calibration.

fields.hypothesis: Deploying a diffusion-multiple approach combined with in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) and time-resolved calorimetry can yield accurate and efficient mapping of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across different HEA compositions.
fields.material_initial_state: A compositionally graded diffusion multiple sample that contains a continuum of HEA compositions (e.g., varying ratios of refractory elements) fabricated via diffusion bonding or additive manufacturing.
fields.intervention: Introduce a controlled composition gradient in a single sample (diffusion multiple) and subject it to simultaneous heating while performing in-situ synchrotron XRD to monitor lattice parameters and phase evolution, concurrently with high-time-resolution calorimetric measurements.
fields.conditions: Heating under constant pressure with rapid time resolution, using high-flux synchrotron sources to capture real-time XRD patterns, while calorimetry records enthalpy changes. The system should cover a wide range of compositions representative of the HEA family.

fields.mechanism: In-situ synchrotron XRD provides precise lattice parameter measurements that reflect the volume changes at melting, while time-resolved calorimetry directly captures heat flow associated with the latent fusion process. By correlating XRD-detected discontinuities (e.g., sudden shift or disappearance of diffraction peaks) with calorimetric anomalies, one can accurately determine both the melting temperature and thermodynamic parameters (enthalpy, entropy of fusion). The diffusion multiple aspect enables systematic mapping across compositions in a single experiment, ensuring efficiency and broad applicability.
fields.predicted_outcome: Distinct and correlated XRD signatures (peak disappearance or significant broadening) and calorimetric peaks should identify the melting transitions within ±10 K. The latent heat determined should be within 5–10% error compared to pure component references, and volume changes should match the XRD-derived densities.
fields.baseline: Sequential measurements on individually fabricated HEA samples using conventional DSC and ex-situ XRD, which are time consuming and less compositionally diverse.
fields.boundary: Primarily applicable to HEAs that can be fabricated as diffusion multiples with gradual compositional variation and where high-flux synchrotron access is available.
fields.uncertainty: Combining data from two in-situ techniques requires careful synchronization and calibration; potential composition-dependent scattering effects in XRD may introduce uncertainty in volume change determination.

measurements: Temperature-resolved XRD patterns (lattice parameters, peak intensities).
Calorimetric heat flow data for latent heat extraction.
Mapping of composition vs. melting temperature and enthalpy.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the XRD signatures and calorimetric data do not correlate to provide a consistent melting temperature and latent heat across the composition gradient, or if the measured values do not conform to expected trends from pure or binary systems, then the method does not yield accurate thermodynamic properties.

fields.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements may vary, depending on the alloy's response to levitation and the synchronization of radiographic imaging; initial estimates are based on known improvements in containerless processing.

Volume change at melting

fields.hypothesis: Extend the Monte Carlo framework by incorporating liquid-state vibrational contributions via molecular dynamics (MD) to simulate the melting transition in HEAs. fields.intervention: Computationally couple Monte Carlo simulations (for configurational contributions) with MD-based phonon/vibrational calculations near the melting point to incorporate the additional entropy and enthalpy contributions from liquid disorder and vibrational modes.

fields.mechanism: At melting, vibrational entropy and anharmonic effects become critical. Incorporating these contributions explicitly allows the simulation to more accurately capture the latent heat and volume change associated with the melting process. The molecular dynamics component simulates the increased atomic displacements and broken periodicity in the liquid, leading to a better estimation of ΔHfusion and ΔSfusion.
fields.predicted_outcome: Accurate predictions of Tm, melting enthalpy, and entropy to within about ±10% of experimentally measured values over the HEA compositional range studied.
fields.baseline: Current Monte Carlo methods based solely on near-neighbor interactions do not capture vibrational contributions, leading to errors in the melting parameters.
fields.boundary: This approach is expected to be applicable for HEA systems where melting occurs from a BCC or partially ordered state; systems with strong short-range order persisting in the liquid might require further adaptation.
fields.uncertainty: The magnitude of vibrational contributions in the complex liquid state is not precisely known; although the approach is physically sound, quantitative uncertainty may remain for alloys with very strong chemical short-range order.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform containerless laser-heating experiments on selected HEAs to precisely measure melting temperature, latent heat, and volume change (using in situ neutron diffraction and high-speed imaging). In parallel, run the coupled Monte Carlo/MD simulations for the same compositions.
measurements: Melting temperature from cooling curve inflections
Latent heat via DSC using levitated droplets
Volume change measured by high-speed X-ray or neutron imaging
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the computed predictions differ from the measured Tm, ΔHfusion, or volume change by more than ~15%, the approach is falsified for that alloy system.

fields.hypothesis: Integrate high-sensitivity calorimetry with in-situ neutron imaging to simultaneously detect latent heat and phase change, enabling accurate extraction of melting temperature, enthalpy, and entropy of fusion in high-entropy alloys.
fields.material_initial_state: Pre-prepared HEA buttons (e.g., equiatomic CoCrCu or CoCrCuNi) fabricated via arc-melting as used in the paper.

fields.mechanism: At the phase transition, latent heat is absorbed (endothermic) without a temperature increase, producing a measurable plateau in the calorimetry trace. Simultaneously, the neutron radiographs capture the spatial and temporal evolution of the melting front. The correlation of these data allows the direct extraction of the melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion (ΔHm), and, via the relation ΔS = ΔHm/Tm, the entropy of fusion.
fields.predicted_outcome: Fusion properties determined with an expected temperature accuracy within ±15 °C and latent heat values measured with an uncertainty potentially within ±5% relative error, subject to sensor calibration.
fields.baseline: Traditional measurements rely on either calorimetry or imaging alone, which can lead to higher uncertainties due to lack of spatial correlation between melting and heat flow.
fields.boundary: Best applicable for homogeneous, single-phase HEAs or alloys where the phase change process is sufficiently abrupt, and where sensor integration does not perturb the temperature field.
fields.uncertainty: Uncertainty in synchronization between the calorimeter signal and imaging data; calibration errors could potentially increase measurement error beyond the expected ranges.

fields.predicted_outcome: Modulated DSC will yield distinct reversible and non-reversible signals, allowing fusion enthalpy (and derived entropy) to be determined with reduced error (targeting ±5% accuracy). fields.boundary: This method is most effective for HEAs where the melting transition is not significantly obscured by overlapping phase transformations; alloys with very rapid crystallization kinetics may still pose challenges.
fields.uncertainty: While the separation of reversible and non-reversible contributions is expected to improve accuracy, quantifying the exact improvement in precision (e.g., ±5% error margins) depends on the specific calorimetric and dilatometric setups and may vary among different HEAs.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If modulated DSC does not show a clear separation between reversible and latent heat components, or if the dilatometry does not detect the expected volume changes coinciding with the DSC signals, then the hypothesis is disproved.

fields.material_initial_state: As-cast, polycrystalline high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with refractory elements (e.g., Cr, Nb, Ti, V, Zr) having potential segregation issues.
fields.intervention: Process the HEA specimens using electromagnetic levitation to achieve containerless melting, with rapid laser heating and simultaneous differential calorimetric measurements.
fields.conditions: Experiments conducted under high-purity inert gas or vacuum, with controlled heating rates (e.g., >10^3 K/s) to reach the melting temperature avoiding prolonged dwell times, and using in situ diagnostics.
fields.structural_mediator: Elimination of contact-induced nucleation and contamination allows the HEA’s inherent thermodynamic behavior to be observed without extrinsic effects.
fields.mechanism: Containerless processing prevents crucible-induced heterogeneous nucleation and minimizes surface oxidation and elemental segregation (such as Zr segregation observed in the paper, record IDs PMC5848872::web::000 and PMC5848872::web::006). This leads to a more uniform melt and consistent latent heat release, enabling accurate determination of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and volume change at melting.
fields.predicted_outcome: A reduced measurement uncertainty in fusion enthalpy (potentially a 10–20% improvement in precision relative to conventional methods) and a more reproducible melting temperature across the HEA family.
fields.baseline: Conventional arc melting and container-based DSC measurements, which suffer from segregation and contamination artifacts as observed in the referenced study.
fields.boundary: This approach is applicable to HEAs that can be processed in levitation systems; its effectiveness may be limited for alloys that are highly reactive or require extremely high temperatures beyond current levitation capabilities.
fields.uncertainty: The quantitative improvement in measurement accuracy is expected but the exact percentage benefit may vary with alloy composition and experimental setup.

fields.hypothesis: Utilize ultra-fast differential scanning calorimetry (flash DSC) to capture the melting transition of HEAs, thereby minimizing the time available for non-equilibrium segregation and phase decomposition.
fields.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys synthesized via arc melting that typically develop non-equilibrium microstructures (e.g., Zr-rich domains as seen in PMC5848872::web::006).
fields.intervention: Implement flash DSC with heating rates in excess of 10^3–10^4 K/s to rapidly traverse the melting range, while concurrently recording high-resolution heat flow.
fields.conditions: Measurements performed under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation, with sample masses in microgram range to ensure uniform temperature distribution and fast response.
fields.structural_mediator: Ultra-fast heating limits diffusion-driven segregation and phase transformations during the measurement, capturing thermodynamic properties at pseudo-equilibrium conditions at the onset of melting.
fields.mechanism: High heating rates suppress diffusion processes and minimize the extent of non-equilibrium microstructural changes (e.g., Zr segregation from Laves phase decomposition noted at around 1000 °C in the paper) during the DSC scan. fields.predicted_outcome: More precise measurement of the melting temperature, enthalpy, and entropy of fusion with reduced scattering in DSC curves; expected improvement in data reproducibility and accuracy compared to conventional DSC by approximately 10–30% in precision, although exact values depend on alloy composition.
fields.baseline: Standard DSC measurements with moderate heating rates that allow for significant microstructural evolution and segregation, leading to deviations from equilibrium thermodynamic values.
fields.boundary: This technique is best suited for alloys whose thermal response is not too sluggish; extremely sluggish kinetics or very high-melting alloys may challenge the sensitivity limits of flash DSC.
fields.uncertainty: While improved precision is anticipated, the exact quantitative enhancement in accuracy may vary across the HEA family.

fields.intervention: Apply laser heating for rapid, localized temperature control while conducting time-resolved synchrotron XRD measurements to observe phase transitions and measure lattice parameters during melting.

fields.predicted_outcome: Accurate, real-time determination of melting temperature, enthalpy, entropy, and volume change with an improved resolution (potentially reducing uncertainty by roughly 15–25% compared to ex situ methods), applicable across varied HEA compositions.

fields.boundary: The approach requires access to synchrotron facilities and may be limited by the spatial resolution of the beam and the laser heating uniformity over larger samples; however, it is particularly suited for small, well-prepared micro-samples.

fields.hypothesis: Deploying a diffusion-multiple approach combined with in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction (XRD) and time-resolved calorimetry can yield accurate and efficient mapping of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy/entropy, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across different HEA compositions.
fields.material_initial_state: A compositionally graded diffusion multiple sample that contains a continuum of HEA compositions (e.g., varying ratios of refractory elements) fabricated via diffusion bonding or additive manufacturing.
fields.intervention: Introduce a controlled composition gradient in a single sample (diffusion multiple) and subject it to simultaneous heating while performing in-situ synchrotron XRD to monitor lattice parameters and phase evolution, concurrently with high-time-resolution calorimetric measurements.
fields.conditions: Heating under constant pressure with rapid time resolution, using high-flux synchrotron sources to capture real-time XRD patterns, while calorimetry records enthalpy changes. The system should cover a wide range of compositions representative of the HEA family.
fields.structural_mediator: Real-time alterations in the crystalline lattice (e.g., lattice expansion, peak broadening/shifts) that signal the onset of melting and atomic rearrangements.
fields.mechanism: In-situ synchrotron XRD provides precise lattice parameter measurements that reflect the volume changes at melting, while time-resolved calorimetry directly captures heat flow associated with the latent fusion process. By correlating XRD-detected discontinuities (e.g., sudden shift or disappearance of diffraction peaks) with calorimetric anomalies, one can accurately determine both the melting temperature and thermodynamic parameters (enthalpy, entropy of fusion). The diffusion multiple aspect enables systematic mapping across compositions in a single experiment, ensuring efficiency and broad applicability.
fields.predicted_outcome: Distinct and correlated XRD signatures (peak disappearance or significant broadening) and calorimetric peaks should identify the melting transitions within ±10 K. The latent heat determined should be within 5–10% error compared to pure component references, and volume changes should match the XRD-derived densities.
fields.baseline: Sequential measurements on individually fabricated HEA samples using conventional DSC and ex-situ XRD, which are time consuming and less compositionally diverse.
fields.boundary: Primarily applicable to HEAs that can be fabricated as diffusion multiples with gradual compositional variation and where high-flux synchrotron access is available.
fields.uncertainty: Combining data from two in-situ techniques requires careful synchronization and calibration; potential composition-dependent scattering effects in XRD may introduce uncertainty in volume change determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a diffusion multiple containing a gradient of HEA compositions. Perform in-situ synchrotron XRD and time-resolved calorimetry during controlled heating. Analyze XRD for disappearance or shifts of diffraction peaks and compare the temperature of these changes with the calorimetric heat-flow anomalies across different regions of the sample.
measurements: Temperature-resolved XRD patterns (lattice parameters, peak intensities).
Calorimetric heat flow data for latent heat extraction.
Mapping of composition vs. melting temperature and enthalpy.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the XRD signatures and calorimetric data do not correlate to provide a consistent melting temperature and latent heat across the composition gradient, or if the measured values do not conform to expected trends from pure or binary systems, then the method does not yield accurate thermodynamic properties.

top3.label: C18
top3.builds_on: The finding and approach of accelerated screening via calculated phase diagrams from the paper (PMC4366518), extending its computational credibility to the fusion property domain.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes to directly couple high-throughput, containerless calorimetric measurements with CALPHAD predictions to extract fusion thermodynamics, rather than only screening phase diagrams.

fields.hypothesis: Integrate high-throughput, containerless differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) with CALPHAD predictions to rapidly determine fusion properties of HEAs.
fields.material_initial_state: A library of high-entropy alloy samples (ranging from ternary to 6-component equimolar alloys) prepared as small, levitated droplets to avoid contamination.
fields.intervention: Implement containerless DSC experiments (e.g., electromagnetic or aerodynamic levitation) that subject individual HEA samples to fast, controlled heating and cooling cycles while simultaneously recording heat flow and volume changes.
fields.conditions: Measurements performed under controlled inert atmospheres at constant pressure; scan rates calibrated for near-equilibrium capture; integration with CALPHAD-derived phase diagrams to select credible compositions.
fields.structural_mediator: Liquid–solid phase interface dynamics measured by DSC together with in situ imaging of droplet shape/volume, serving as a proxy for volume change at melting.
fields.mechanism: Containerless processing minimizes heterogeneous nucleation and sample contamination, ensuring that the measured heat flow (latent heat/fusion) and volume changes reflect intrinsic thermodynamic properties. Coupling the measured DSC data with CALPHAD predictions exploits pre-existing thermodynamic databases and phase diagram information to constrain melting temperature (Tm), enthalpy and entropy of fusion.
fields.predicted_outcome: Accurate determination of Tm within ±5% and fusion enthalpy/entropy values with similar error margins; observed volume changes consistent with underlying atomic size variations predicted by CALPHAD analysis. Expected performance improvement is an order‐of‐magnitude increase in throughput compared to conventional methods.
fields.baseline: Traditional DSC on bulk samples and standard container-based methods that suffer from contamination and thermal gradients.
fields.boundary: The approach is applicable to HEAs where CALPHAD databases are reliable (fAB = 1 systems) and may be limited for compositions with very complex phase behavior or extremely low thermal stability.
fields.uncertainty: The calibration of levitated droplet DSC for very rapid transitions may introduce uncertainties if the sample’s heat transfer kinetics differ from bulk behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform containerless DSC measurements on a set of HEA samples and compare the measured melting temperatures and latent heats with CALPHAD predictions. Independently determine the volume change at melting using high-speed imaging of droplet deformation.
measurements: DSC heat flow curves
Temperature profiles
Droplet volume change via image analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured Tm, ΔHfusion, ΔSfusion, and volume change values differ systematically (>±15%) from the CALPHAD-calibrated predictions and cannot be reconciled by known kinetic effects, the hypothesis is ruled out.

top3.label: C1
top3.builds_on: the MC/MD and bond-counting thermodynamic approaches used in the paper
top3.what_is_new: It integrates an ML‐enhanced interatomic potential framework—calibrated using ab initio data in both solid and liquid regimes—to accurately capture SRC behavior across the phase boundary, an aspect not addressed in the original work.

fields.hypothesis: Develop a multi‐scale simulation framework that employs machine‐learning corrected interatomic potentials, validated against ab initio molecular dynamics data in both solid and liquid regimes, to accurately capture the evolution (and dissolution) of SRCs across the solid–liquid interface in HEAs.
fields.material_initial_state: An annealed, equimolar HEA such as TaNbHfZr that exhibits equilibrium short‐range chemical ordering (SRC) in the solid state.
fields.intervention: Generate a high-temperature ab initio MD dataset covering both solid and liquid phases of the HEA. Train and incorporate a machine-learning correction (e.g., using Gaussian approximation potentials or similar) onto a standard EAM potential to ensure its transferability across phases. Use this ML‐corrected potential in two-phase coexistence simulations to resolve melting temperature, latent heat, fusion entropy, and volume change.
fields.conditions: Simulations conducted in an isobaric ensemble near the expected fusion temperature with sufficiently large cells (e.g., >50,000 atoms) to capture spatial variations and SRC effects; calibration performed over a temperature range spanning the solid–liquid transition.
fields.structural_mediator: The structural evolution and partial retention (or gradual dissolution) of SRC regions at the interface, which directly affect local configurational and vibrational free energy contributions.
fields.mechanism: By accurately capturing interatomic interactions in both phases, the ML‐enhanced potential reproduces the influence of SRCs on the energy landscape. This multi‐scale approach allows robust free energy integration across the phase boundary so that the computed Tm, ΔHfusion, ΔSfusion, and volume change reflect both the chemical ordering of the solid and the disordered liquid state.
fields.predicted_outcome: Fusion properties (melting temperature, latent heat, and fusion entropy) are expected to be predicted with an error margin in the order of 5–10% when compared with calibrated experimental measurements. SRC‐mediated contributions to the free energy will be clearly resolved.
fields.baseline: Previous simulations used standard EAM potentials calibrated for the solid state without verified accuracy in the liquid state.
fields.boundary: This approach is applicable to HEA systems for which reliable ab initio data can be generated and where local SRC effects are crucial but not overwhelmingly complex; systems exhibiting extreme phase separation may require additional modeling.
fields.uncertainty: The quality and transferability of the ML‐corrected potential depend on the comprehensiveness of the ab initio dataset. Uncertainty remains in quantifying the precise impact of SRC dissolution on liquid-phase properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct ML‐corrected two‐phase coexistence simulations for a TaNbHfZr HEA and compute Tm, ΔHfusion, ΔSfusion and volume change. Independently, conduct high-temperature calorimetric and dilatometric experiments on well-characterized samples. Compare the simulation results with experimental data.

Calculated latent heat per atom
Derived fusion entropy
Volume change across the melting transition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted fusion properties deviate by more than ~10% from the experimental benchmarks or if the simulation fails to resolve a consistent trend in SRC evolution at the interface, the hypothesis is falsified.
